long_biography.plain_text:
Within months of being dismissed by Henry Ford II, Lee Iacocca accepted responsibility for a Chrysler Corporation nearing collapse. He closed plants, negotiated concessions from labour and lenders, and persuaded Congress to back $1.5 billion in loan guarantees. The K-cars and a new minivan family then helped rebuild sales. Repaying the guaranteed loans seven years early turned Iacocca into a corporate celebrity whose blunt television advertisements made him unusually recognisable.

Iacocca's judgment had been shaped across three decades at Ford. An Allentown-born son of Italian immigrants, he trained as an engineer but soon asked to move into sales. His “56 for 56” financing campaign demonstrated a talent for pairing products with a marketable proposition. He later helped bring the Mustang to customers and climbed to the automaker's top operating post. After retirement, he led fundraising for the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island restorations. His wife Mary's death also prompted the creation of a family foundation devoted to diabetes research.
